> There's a new assertion in [attempt to populate the history entry's document](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/browsing-the-web.html#attempt-to-populate-the-history-entry's-document) that is firing in a navigation from about:blank to about:srcdoc. Do we only trip the assert when going from `about:blank` to `about:srcdoc`, as you suggest? I feel like we might be hitting this on all `about:srcdoc` navigations. ---- I like the idea of setting document state's referrer explicitly in `#navigate` so we don't satisfy the `request referrer is "client"` condition, and thus we avoid the assert. However, the details are interesting. I'm not sure if we'd want to manually set the request referrer for both `about:blank` and `about:srcdoc` navs, or just `about:srcdoc` navs. If we decide to set the document state's request referrer for `about:blank` navigations (not just srcdoc), we might consider doing the same in ["create a new top-level traversable"](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/C#creating-a-new-top-level-traversable) when _opener_ is provided—that algorithm is almost like navigation, in that it creates a new top-level traversable whose Document [gets its referrer set to the opener's URL](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/C#creating-browsing-contexts:the-document's-referrer), but whose document state [does not save the referrer](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/C#top-level-traversables:document-state-2).
Here's why I don't think we should set document state's referrer in the "new top-level traversable" case If we were to save the referrer in the document state too for the "new top-level traversable" case, I guess this would change the behavior of bf-cache-restored (and maybe session history restored more generally?) `about:blank` Documents, since they would suddenly have a `document.referrer` when they don't today, per spec. But I don't think we should do this, because it looks like browsers don't even follow the spec when it comes to the simpler case of setting `window.open`ed-`about:blank` Document's referrer in the first place. Navigate to `example.com` and run `window.open("", "_blank")` and you see: | | Chrome | Firefox | Safari | | -------- | -------- | ------- | ------- | |`document.referrer`|`https://example.com`|`""`|`""`| So as expected, if you close the `about:blank` tab and then resurrect with `CMD+SHIFT+T` or something, you get: | | Chrome | Firefox | Safari | | -------- | -------- | ------- | ------- | |`document.referrer`|`""`|`""`|`""`| So I guess we shouldn't touch the "new top-level traversable" case. That means we can either set the document state's referrer in the `about:blank` _navigation_ case (not creation case), and live with the minor inconsistency between those two, or set it for `about:srcdoc` only.
Another option—instead of committing anything new to the document state—would be to tighten the 6.7.3 "If entry's document state's request referrer is "client", and navigationParams is a navigation params" condition, to exclude URLs that [require storing the policy container in history](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/browsers.html#requires-storing-the-policy-container-in-history), thus avoiding the assert for `about:srcdoc` navigations. I think this path might be a little better, since when you navigate an iframe to `data:text/html,

test`, I don't observe `document.referrer` being set or saved to the document state at all. So this approach might better match what browsers are doing. Do you think this path sounds good @domenic? If we go that second path, we still have an issue where browsers are apparently never running [the step that sets the actual Document's referrer](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/document-lifecycle.html#shared-document-creation-infrastructure:the-document's-referrer-2) at least for local URLs like `about:blank`, `about:srcdoc`, and `data:` URLs.

> Do you think this path sounds good @domenic?

I think it sounds reasonable.

But, I want to take a step back though and clarify what we're trying to accomplish, especially in the more general case. E.g. you say 

> Browsers are apparently never running [the step that sets the actual Document's referrer](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/document-lifecycle.html#shared-document-creation-infrastructure:the-document's-referrer-2) at least for local URLs like `about:blank`, `about:srcdoc`, and `data:` URLs.

but per your test results you mean Firefox and Safari are not, right? Chrome is?

IIUC there are the following interesting cases here:

1. "Fresh" top-level traversables, created e.g. by the user.
2. "New" but non-fresh top-level traversables, created e.g. by `window.open("about:blank", "_blank")` or `window.open("https://example.com/", "_blank")`.
3. Nested `about:blank` navigables, created e.g. by `<iframe src="about:blank">`.
4. Nested `about:srcdoc` navigables, created by `<iframe srcdoc>`.

(1) should definitely not get a referrer set on their document.

For (2)-(4), I could go either way. There's clearly something that's creating them, so setting a referrer from that seems kind of reasonable. But there's no "request" (certainly no actual HTTP request over the network), so having no referrer also makes sense.

It would be vaguely nice if we could get consistency between (2)-(4), or at least between (3)-(4). It sounds like that might be possible?

> but per your test results you mean Firefox and Safari are not, right? Chrome is? Actually no! In the `
` in my last comment, I record that Chrome is the only browser that implements ["create a new browsing context and document" Step 16.1](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/document-sequences.html#creating-browsing-contexts%3Athe-document's-referrer): `document.referrer` assignment in the new-but-non-fresh-top-level traversable case. But when I wrote: > If we go that second path, we still have an issue where browsers are apparently never running [the step that sets the actual Document's referrer](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/document-lifecycle.html#shared-document-creation-infrastructure:the-document's-referrer-2) at least for local URLs like about:blank, about:srcdoc, and data: URLs. I am referring to the normal shared document creation steps that runs after navigations, including for nested navigables. For example, go to https://web-kitchen.glitch.me and click `Load example.com` and inspect the iframe's `document.referrer`. Do the same after clicking `Load about:blank`, `Load blob: URL`, and again after loading a srcdoc manually (site doesn't support that yet). Here are the complete `document.referrer` results I see for nested navigables, and new-but-non-fresh-top-level navigables:
Navigation type Navigation destination Chrome Firefox Safari
Load in iframe 'example.com' 'https://web-kitchen.glitch.me/' 'https://web-kitchen.glitch.me/' 'https://web-kitchen.glitch.me/'
'about:blank' '' '' ''
'srcdoc=foo' '' '' ''
'data: URL' '' '' ''
'blob: URL' '' '' ''
window.open(..,"_blank") 'example.com' 'https://web-kitchen.glitch.me/' 'https://web-kitchen.glitch.me/' 'https://web-kitchen.glitch.me/'
'about:blank' 'https://web-kitchen.glitch.me/' '' ''
'blob: URL' '' '' ''
Let's proceed with these results in mind. > (1) should definitely not get a referrer set on their document. Agreed; I don't think this was ever on the table. In the totally fresh case, there is no referrer/creator/opener/predecessor thing at all, so `document.referrer` should just be blank. > For (2)-(4), I could go either way. There's clearly something that's creating them, so setting a referrer from that seems kind of reasonable. But there's no "request" (certainly no actual HTTP request over the network), so having no referrer also makes sense. Well not entirely, since part of your (2) example includes `example.com` which involves a legitimate HTTP request. But if we remove that sub-case, then I agree it would be nice if we could get consistency between everything in (2)-(4), since they are all "local" resources. In fact, I think it's better to group things by resource kind (local vs non-local) rather than navigation type (`window.open()` vs nested navigable), and the table above shows us that we have almost perfect alignment on this, except for Chrome being the odd one out in assigning `document.referrer` in the new-non-fresh navigable case. So it seems like the path of least resistance is: 1. Deleting ["create a new browsing context and document" Step 16.1](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/document-sequences.html#creating-browsing-contexts%3Athe-document's-referrer) and changing Chrome to agree with the other browsers 2. Do something similar to what I recommended in ["Another option"](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/10099#user-content-another-option) above, but maybe we just tighten to exclude _all_ local URLs period. Thoughts?

> So it seems like the path of least resistance is:

This sounds great to me! Thanks for the thorough analysis.

OK so there's something wrong in the above analysis. The HTML Standard has two places where a new Document's referrer is assigned:
  1. Navigable creation case: ["create a new browsing context and document" Step 16.1](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/C#creating-browsing-contexts:the-document's-referrer)
  2. Navigation case: ["create and initialize a Document object" Step 12.3](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/C#shared-document-creation-infrastructure:the-document's-referrer-2)

Looking back, I believe for iframes I only exercised the _navigation case_, because in all of the iframe navigations above, I record that I came to the results by visiting https://web-kitchen.glitch.me and clicking buttons that navigate an existing iframe. There is basically no distinction between the _creation case_ and _navigation case_ except for `about:blank`, since for all other URLs, you can only arrive at them from via navigation.

When going back and testing the `about:blank` _creation case_, I realize I missed that both Chrome and Safari actually do implement ["create a new browsing context and document" Step 16.1](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/C#creating-browsing-contexts:the-document's-referrer). Chrome has done this for a long time, and Safari fixed its implementation in https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/pull/20158, as indicated in https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=242965. You can see this in the following WPT results:

 - https://wpt.fyi/results/html/browsers/windows/browsing-context.html
 - https://wpt.fyi/results/referrer-policy/generic/inheritance/iframe-inheritance-about-blank.html
 - https://wpt.fyi/results/referrer-policy/generic/inheritance/popup-inheritance-about-blank.html
    - Safari actually fails this test, but not because they're trying to exclude the entire referrer like Firefox (empty string). They just fail because they use the inherited referrer policy to redact the `document.referrer`, even though the spec does not consult the referrer policy for newly created navigables. I've reopened https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=242965 to track this.

So that leaves us with 2/3 browsers implementing creator referrer assignment on the initial about:blank Document, so I think we should close https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/10883 as Wontfix.

----

That leaves us with the main part of this bug, and the approach I outlined in the second bullet of my last message:

> 2. Do something similar to what I recommended in ["Another option"](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/10099#user-content-another-option above), but maybe we just tighten to exclude all local URLs period.

To add some color to this, I think this will require two changes:

1. First, tighten up https://html.spec.whatwg.org/C#populating-a-session-history-entry:document-state-request-referrer to exclude all [local](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#is-local) URLs, so that referrer information isn't saved to the document state
2. Probably add the same check to https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#shared-document-creation-infrastructure:the-document's-referrer-2, to tighten _it_ up to ensure that Documents with the URLs with local URLs in the table (in the last message) have empty `document.referrer`s regardless of their referring document.

This sounds right. To be clear I understand:

> 1. First, tighten up https://html.spec.whatwg.org/C#populating-a-session-history-entry:document-state-request-referrer to exclude all [local](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#is-local) URLs, so that referrer information isn't saved to the document state

This is about fixing the assert, by not attempting to look at the request's referrer when there's no request.

We could alternately fix the assert by checking if the request is null, and only storing referrer information if there's a request. This would result in storing referrer information for some local URL cases (`data:`, etc.) but not for the srcdoc case (which has null request).

It's a little strange to not store referrer information in the document state here. The point of document state is to be useful when re-doing a request. And for cases like `data:` URLs, we do in theory re-do the request. So in theory it would be useful to save that referrer. But per your testing, it sounds like browsers do not end up using the referrer, or at least not propagating it to the created document. So whether or not we save it here is not really relevant, and maybe it's clearer if we don't save it.

For these cases, we could consider intentionally storing "no-referrer" there, instead of leaving it as "client". It doesn't matter too much. Whatever value we send to fetch mostly isn't relevant for local URLs, since there's no server to actually receive and care about the `Referer` header.

> 2\. Probably add the same check to https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#shared-document-creation-infrastructure:the-document's-referrer-2, to tighten _it_ up to ensure that Documents with the URLs with local URLs in the table (in the last message) have empty `document.referrer`s regardless of their referring document.

This is about fixing `document.referrer` for the new documents to match web reality.

There are several levels we could do this at:

- We could do it like you suggest, and update the Document creation to not copy over the referrer from the request.
- We could ensure the request never has a referrer at the HTML level, by combining the above idea of storing "no-referrer" in the document state, _plus_ something else that sets the referrer policy or referrer for all navigations to local URLs. (The former takes care of restoring from history, the latter takes care of the initial navigation.)
- We could ensure the request never has a referrer at the Fetch level, by modifying the Fetch spec.

The final option seems slightly nicer to me (/cc @annevk), but the first option is certainly easier.

> Whatever value we send to fetch mostly isn't relevant for local URLs

Agreed, though one could imagine this getting exposed in some side channel API at some point at which point we do need the clarity.

---

These three options are all intriguing and none of them jump out to me as a clear winner.

1. This seems the most robust option and I think ideally we at the very least add an Assert there to keep the rest of the system honest.
2. I wonder if the inverse works better. That we only set referrer for HTTP(S) requests. But still this seems like a lot of busy work for HTML.
3. Adjusting the referrer is already done in Fetch, so it makes sense to me to continue tweaking it there (or perhaps in Referrer Policy as Fetch does call out to that). If we never need it for non-HTTP(S) URLs, let's make it so.
